sparkling-wine.title: Kir Royale
sparkling-wine.intro: A sophisticated and festive cocktail, the Kir Royale elevates sparkling wine with a touch of blackcurrant liqueur. It's a perfect elegant toast for New Year's Day celebrations, adding a touch of French chic to your festive gatherings, and an ideal aperitif for an evening of cultural enjoyment, such as attending "The Magic Flute."
ingredients: 0.5 fluid ounce (15 ml) Crème de Cassis (blackcurrant liqueur)
5 fluid ounces (150 ml) chilled dry sparkling wine (e.g., Brut Champagne, Cava, Prosecco)
Optional: 1 fresh raspberry or lemon twist for garnish
steps: Pour the Crème de Cassis into a chilled flute glass.
Slowly top with the chilled sparkling wine.
If desired, garnish with a fresh raspberry or a lemon twist.
Serve immediately.
tips: Use a good quality, dry sparkling wine for the best flavor balance.
Chill both the Crème de Cassis and the sparkling wine thoroughly before serving.
For a non-alcoholic version, use blackcurrant syrup and sparkling cider or non-alcoholic sparkling wine.

hoppin-john.title: Hoppin' John
hoppin-john.intro: Hoppin' John is a traditional Southern dish made with black-eyed peas and rice, often served with collard greens and cornbread. It is a staple on New Year's Day, believed to bring good luck and prosperity for the coming year, with the peas symbolizing coins and the greens representing paper money.
ingredients: 6 cups (1.4 L) chicken or vegetable broth
1 tablespoon (15ml) olive oil or bacon fat
4 ounces (113g) smoked ham hock, bacon, or salt pork, diced
Salt and freshly ground black pepper to taste
Fresh parsley or green onions, chopped, for garnish
steps: Rinse the dried black-eyed peas thoroughly. For quicker cooking, soak them in cold water overnight, then drain. Alternatively, use the quick-soak method: cover peas with water, bring to a boil for 10 minutes, then remove from heat and let stand for 1 hour, then drain.

In a large Dutch oven or heavy-bottomed pot, heat the olive oil or bacon fat over medium heat. Add the diced ham hock, bacon, or salt pork and cook until crispy, about 5-7 minutes. Remove the meat with a slotted spoon and set aside, leaving the rendered fat in the pot.
Add the chopped onion, green bell pepper, and celery to the pot. Sauté until softened, about 8-10 minutes.
Stir in the minced garlic, dried thyme, smoked paprika, and cayenne pepper (if using). Cook for 1 minute until fragrant.

Add the drained black-eyed peas, chicken or vegetable broth, and bay leaf to the pot. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to low, cover, and simmer for 45-60 minutes, or until the peas are tender but not mushy. Stir occasionally.
Once the peas are tender, stir in the long-grain white rice and the reserved cooked meat (if using bacon or salt pork, ham hock can remain in the pot). Bring the mixture back to a gentle simmer.

Cover the pot and continue to cook for another 15-20 minutes, or until the rice is tender and has absorbed most of the liquid. If the mixture becomes too dry before the rice is cooked, add a little more broth or water.
Remove the bay leaf. Season with salt and freshly ground black pepper to taste. Let it rest, covered, for 5 minutes before serving.
Garnish with fresh parsley or chopped green onions before serving hot.
tips: For a vegetarian version, omit the ham hock/bacon and use vegetable broth. A dash of liquid smoke can add a smoky flavor.
Serve Hoppin' John with a side of collard greens (for 'money') and cornbread (for 'gold') to complete the traditional New Year's Day meal.
Leftovers are said to be 'Skippin' Jenny' and are considered even luckier the next day.

sausage.title: Pan-Fried Swiss Cervelat with Onions
sausage.intro: Berchtoldstag, celebrated on January 2nd in parts of Switzerland, is a day for gathering with family and friends, often marked by hearty, traditional meals. This simple preparation of Cervelat, Switzerland's national sausage, pan-fried with sweet onions, offers a comforting and flavorful dish perfect for a festive holiday lunch or dinner.
ingredients: 4 large Swiss Cervelat sausages (about 1.5 lb / 680 g total)
1/2 cup (120 ml) beef or vegetable broth
Salt and freshly ground black pepper to taste
steps: Carefully peel the skin off each Cervelat sausage.
Slice each sausage into 1/2-inch (1.25 cm) thick rounds.
In a large skillet or frying pan, melt the butter over medium heat.
Add the sliced onions to the pan and sauté for 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until softened and lightly golden.
Add the sliced Cervelat to the pan with the onions.
Cook for 5-7 minutes, turning occasionally, until the sausage slices are heated through and slightly browned.
Pour in the beef or vegetable broth, scraping up any browned bits from the bottom of the pan.
Bring the broth to a simmer and cook for 2-3 minutes, allowing it to reduce slightly and coat the sausages and onions.
Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Garnish with fresh chopped parsley before serving.
tips: Serve hot with traditional Swiss Rösti, boiled potatoes, or crusty bread to soak up the delicious pan juices.
For an extra touch, add a splash of white wine along with the broth for a richer flavor.
If Cervelat is unavailable, a good quality smoked frankfurter or a mild, cooked German Bratwurst can be a suitable substitute.

longevity-noodles.title: Longevity Noodles with Pork and Vegetables
longevity-noodles.intro: Longevity Noodles, or Changshou Mian, are a staple dish served during New Year's Day and especially Lunar New Year (Chunjie) celebrations. The long strands of noodles symbolize a long life and good fortune, making it customary to eat them without breaking them. This savory, stir-fried dish is a delicious way to usher in a prosperous year.
ingredients: 8 oz (225 g) fresh or dried long egg noodles
8 oz (225 g) pork loin or tenderloin, thinly sliced
1 tablespoon soy sauce, plus more for sauce
1 inch (2.5 cm) ginger, grated or minced
4 dried shiitake mushrooms, rehydrated and sliced (stems removed)
4 oz (115 g) baby bok choy, quartered lengthwise
2 scallions, green parts sliced for garnish
2 tablespoons water or mushroom soaking liquid
steps: In a medium bowl, marinate the thinly sliced pork with 1 tablespoon soy sauce and 1 teaspoon cornstarch. Set aside for at least 15 minutes.
Cook the egg noodles according to package directions until al dente. Drain well, rinse with cold water to prevent sticking, and set aside.
While noodles cook, prepare the sauce by whisking together 2 tablespoons soy sauce, oyster sauce (if using), sesame oil, sugar, and water or mushroom soaking liquid in a small bowl.

Heat 1 tablespoon vegetable oil in a large skillet or wok over medium-high heat. Add the marinated pork and stir-fry until cooked through and lightly browned, about 3-4 minutes. Remove pork from the wok and set aside.
Add the remaining 1 teaspoon vegetable oil to the wok. Add minced garlic and grated ginger, stir-fry for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the sliced shiitake mushrooms and julienned carrots to the wok. Stir-fry for 2-3 minutes until carrots begin to soften.
Add the quartered baby bok choy and stir-fry for another 2 minutes until slightly wilted but still crisp.
Return the cooked pork to the wok with the vegetables. Add the cooked and drained noodles.

Pour the prepared sauce over the noodles and vegetables. Toss everything together gently but thoroughly, ensuring the noodles are evenly coated with the sauce. Cook for 1-2 minutes, allowing the sauce to heat through and coat the ingredients.
Serve immediately, garnished with sliced green scallions. Encourage diners to eat the noodles without breaking them for good luck.
tips: For a vegetarian version, omit the pork and oyster sauce, and add extra vegetables like bell peppers or snow peas. Use vegetable broth instead of mushroom soaking liquid if needed.
Ensure your noodles are long; some Asian markets sell specific 'longevity noodles' that are extra-long.
You can add a touch of chili garlic sauce to the finished dish for a bit of heat, if desired.

king-cake.title: Traditional King Cake
king-cake.intro: King Cake is a festive brioche-like cake, traditionally enjoyed from Twelfth Night (January 6th, Epiphany) through Mardi Gras, marking the end of the Christmas season and the start of Carnival. It's often decorated in purple, green, and gold, symbolizing justice, faith, and power, and famously contains a hidden trinket, bringing luck to the finder.
ingredients: 2 ¼ teaspoons (7 g) active dry yeast (one packet)
½ cup (100 g) granulated sugar, divided
4 ½ cups (540 g) all-purpose flour, plus more for dusting
½ cup (113 g) unsalted butter, melted and cooled
2-3 tablespoons (30-45 ml) milk or lemon juice
Purple, green, and gold sanding sugars
1 small plastic baby or dried bean
steps: In a large bowl, combine the warm milk, active dry yeast, and 1 tablespoon of the granulated sugar. Let stand for 5-10 minutes until foamy.
In a separate large bowl, whisk together the all-purpose flour, remaining granulated sugar, salt, ground nutmeg, and lemon zest (if using).
Add the beaten eggs and melted butter to the yeast mixture. Gradually add the dry ingredients to the wet ingredients, mixing until a shaggy dough forms.
Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and knead for 8-10 minutes, until smooth and elastic.
Place the dough in a lightly oiled bowl, turning once to coat. Cover with plastic wrap and let rise in a warm place for 1-1.5 hours, or until doubled in size.
While the dough rises, prepare the filling: Beat the softened cream cheese, ½ cup granulated sugar, and 1 teaspoon vanilla extract together until smooth and creamy.
Punch down the risen dough. On a lightly floured surface, roll the dough into a large rectangle, approximately 12x18 inches (30x45 cm).
Spread the cream cheese filling evenly over the dough, leaving a 1-inch (2.5 cm) border on one long edge.
Starting from the long edge opposite the border, tightly roll the dough into a log. Bring the ends of the log together to form an oval ring, pinching them firmly to seal.
Carefully transfer the ring to a parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover loosely with plastic wrap or a clean kitchen towel and let rise in a warm place for another 45-60 minutes, or until puffy.
Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Bake for 35-40 minutes, or until golden brown. If browning too quickly, you can loosely tent with foil.
Let the cake cool completely on a wire rack before icing.
Prepare the icing: In a small bowl, whisk together the powdered sugar, 2-3 tablespoons milk (or lemon juice), and ½ teaspoon vanilla extract until smooth. Adjust milk for desired consistency.
Drizzle or spread the icing over the cooled cake. Immediately sprinkle with purple, green, and gold sanding sugars in alternating sections.
Once the cake is decorated, carefully insert the plastic baby or dried bean into the underside of the cake.
tips: Ensure your yeast is fresh and your milk is at the correct temperature for a good rise.
For a richer dough, you can use whole milk instead of lower-fat milk.
The hidden trinket is traditionally a small plastic baby, symbolizing the baby Jesus. The person who finds it is said to have good luck and is often responsible for hosting the next King Cake party.

fondue.title: Traditional Swiss Cheese Fondue
fondue.intro: Swiss Cheese Fondue is a beloved communal dish, perfect for the festive atmosphere of Berchtoldstag on January 2nd. This holiday, celebrated in several Swiss cantons, is a time for family and friends to gather, and a warm, bubbling pot of fondue provides a cozy and interactive centerpiece for winter celebrations, symbolizing togetherness and good cheer.
ingredients: 2 cups (470 ml) dry white wine (such as Fendant or Sauvignon Blanc)
1-2 loaves crusty day-old bread (such as baguette or rustic white bread), cut into 1-inch (2.5 cm) cubes
steps: Rub the inside of a heavy-bottomed pot (a 'caquelon' if you have one) thoroughly with the peeled garlic clove, then discard the garlic.
In a small bowl, whisk together the cornstarch and Kirsch until smooth; set aside.
Pour the dry white wine into the garlic-rubbed pot and heat over medium-low heat until it just begins to simmer, but do not boil.

Gradually add the grated Gruyère and Emmentaler cheeses to the wine, a handful at a time, stirring continuously in a figure-eight motion with a wooden spoon until each addition is melted and smooth before adding more.
Once all the cheese is melted and the fondue is creamy, stir in the cornstarch-Kirsch mixture.
Continue to stir gently for 1-2 minutes until the fondue thickens slightly and is smooth and glossy.
Season the fondue with freshly grated nutmeg and a pinch of black pepper.
Carefully transfer the fondue to a preheated fondue pot set over a low flame or burner to keep it warm and bubbling gently.
Serve immediately with the cubed bread for dipping.
tips: To prevent the fondue from separating or becoming stringy, add the cheese gradually and stir constantly in a figure-eight motion.
If the fondue becomes too thick, stir in a tablespoon or two of warm white wine. If it's too thin, mix a little more cornstarch with Kirsch and stir it in.
Traditionally, if someone drops their bread into the fondue, they might owe a round of drinks or a kiss to the person next to them!

hazelnut-torte.title: Berchtoldstag Hazelnut Torte
hazelnut-torte.intro: The Hazelnut Torte, or Haselnusstorte, is a beloved Swiss pastry, perfect for celebrating Berchtoldstag on January 2nd. This holiday, primarily observed in Switzerland, is a time for family gatherings and enjoying rich, comforting treats. This torte, with its buttery crust and sweet, nutty filling, embodies the warmth and tradition of the festive season.
ingredients: 1/2 cup (115 g) unsalted butter, cold and cubed
steps: To make the dough: In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, salt, and lemon zest. Add the cold, cubed butter and cut it into the flour mixture using a pastry blender or your fingertips until it resembles coarse crumbs.
Add the egg and mix until the dough just comes together. Do not overmix. Form the dough into a disc, wrap it in plastic wrap, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes.
To make the filling: In a medium bowl, combine the ground hazelnuts, sugar, heavy cream, honey (or maple syrup), egg yolk, vanilla extract, and cinnamon. Mix well until thoroughly combined.
Preheat your oven to 350°F (175°C). Grease and lightly flour a 9-inch (23 cm) springform pan.
Divide the chilled dough into two portions: one larger (about 2/3 of the dough) for the base and sides, and one smaller (about 1/3) for the top crust.

On a lightly floured surface, roll out the larger dough portion into a circle large enough to cover the bottom and extend up the sides of the prepared springform pan. Carefully transfer the dough to the pan, pressing it gently into the bottom and up the sides.
Spread the hazelnut filling evenly over the dough in the pan.
Roll out the smaller dough portion into a circle slightly larger than the top of the pan. Carefully place it over the filling.
Trim any excess dough from the edges, leaving a small overhang. Crimp the edges of the top and bottom crusts together to seal the torte. You can use a fork to create a decorative edge.
Brush the top of the torte with the beaten egg wash. Using a fork, prick the top crust several times to allow steam to escape during baking.
Bake for 45-55 minutes, or until the crust is golden brown and the filling is set. If the crust starts to brown too quickly, you can loosely cover it with aluminum foil.
Remove the torte from the oven and let it cool completely on a wire rack before removing the springform pan. This is crucial for the torte to set properly.
Once cooled, you may dust the top with powdered sugar before slicing and serving.
tips: For best flavor and texture, allow the torte to cool completely, ideally overnight, before serving. This allows the flavors to meld beautifully.
You can substitute walnuts or almonds for hazelnuts, though it will change the traditional flavor profile.
Store the torte at room temperature, covered, for up to 3-4 days, or refrigerate for longer freshness.

rosti.title: Traditional Rösti for Berchtoldstag
rosti.intro: Rösti is a beloved Swiss potato dish, often described as a giant potato pancake, celebrated for its crispy exterior and tender interior. It's a comforting and hearty meal perfectly suited for Berchtoldstag on January 2nd, a holiday observed in many parts of Switzerland. After the New Year's festivities, a simple yet satisfying dish like Rösti provides warmth and tradition for family gatherings.
ingredients: 2 pounds (about 1 kg) starchy potatoes (like Russet or Yukon Gold)
4 tablespoons (60 ml) unsalted butter or clarified butter (or lard), divided
1 teaspoon (5 ml) salt, or to taste
1/2 teaspoon (2.5 ml) freshly ground black pepper, or to taste
steps: Boil the potatoes in their skins in salted water until just tender when pierced with a fork, about 15-20 minutes depending on size. Do not overcook them until mushy. Drain well and let them cool completely, ideally refrigerating them overnight. Cold potatoes are crucial for the best texture.
Once the potatoes are thoroughly chilled, peel them and grate them using the coarse side of a box grater.
In a large bowl, gently toss the grated potatoes with salt and pepper until evenly seasoned.
Heat a large (10-12 inch or 25-30 cm) heavy-bottomed non-stick or cast-iron skillet over medium heat. Add 2 tablespoons (30 ml) of the butter to the skillet and let it melt until shimmering.
Add all the seasoned grated potatoes to the hot skillet. Using a spatula, press the potatoes down firmly and evenly to form a compact, flat cake. Do not stir or move the potatoes once pressed.
Cook undisturbed for 15-20 minutes, or until a deep golden-brown and crispy crust forms on the bottom. You can gently lift an edge with a spatula to check the color.

To flip the Rösti, place a large, flat plate over the skillet. Carefully and confidently invert the skillet onto the plate, so the Rösti rests on the plate, cooked side up. Add the remaining 2 tablespoons (30 ml) of butter to the skillet, let it melt.
Carefully slide the Rösti from the plate back into the skillet, uncooked side down. Continue cooking for another 10-15 minutes, or until the second side is also deeply golden brown and crisp.
Once both sides are golden and crispy, slide the Rösti onto a serving platter. Cut into wedges and serve immediately.
tips: Using cold, day-old boiled potatoes is the secret to achieving the perfect crispy exterior and fluffy interior of traditional Rösti.
Don't skimp on the fat; it's essential for developing that delicious golden crust. Clarified butter or lard adds authentic flavor.
Rösti is versatile: serve it as a main dish with a fried egg, applesauce, or a dollop of sour cream, or as a hearty side dish to roasted meats.

zopf.title: Zopf
zopf.intro: Zopf, meaning "braid" in Swiss German, is a rich, buttery braided bread that is a beloved staple in Switzerland. Traditionally enjoyed on Sunday mornings, it also holds a special place during holidays like Berchtoldstag, the New Year's Day celebration in many Swiss cantons. Its golden crust and tender crumb make it a comforting and festive start to the new year, often served with butter and jam.
ingredients: 1 cup (240 ml) whole milk, warmed to 105-115°F (40-46°C)
2 ¼ teaspoons (7g) active dry yeast (one standard packet)
4 ½ cups (540g) all-purpose flour, plus more for dusting
½ cup (113g) unsalted butter, melted and cooled
1 large egg, plus 1 egg yolk (for the dough)
steps: In a small bowl, combine the warm milk, yeast, and 1 teaspoon of sugar. Let it sit for 5-10 minutes until foamy.
In a large mixing bowl, whisk together the flour and salt.
Add the melted butter, 1 large egg, and 1 egg yolk to the yeast mixture, and whisk to combine.
Pour the wet ingredients into the dry ingredients and mix with a wooden spoon or stand mixer with a dough hook until a shaggy dough forms.
Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and knead for 8-10 minutes, or use a stand mixer on medium-low speed for 6-8 minutes, until the dough is smooth and elastic.

Lightly grease a clean bowl with oil, place the dough in it, turning once to coat. Cover the bowl with plastic wrap or a clean kitchen towel and let it rise in a warm place for 1.5-2 hours, or until doubled in size.
Punch down the risen dough gently and turn it out onto a lightly floured surface. Divide the dough into two equal pieces.
Roll each piece into a long strand, about 18-20 inches (45-50 cm) long, tapering slightly at the ends.

Place the two strands parallel to each other. Cross the right strand over the left. Then take the new right strand and cross it over the left. Continue this simple over-under pattern, always taking the strand that is now on the right and crossing it over the left, until you reach the end. Pinch the ends together to seal.

Carefully transfer the braided loaf to a baking sheet lined with parchment paper. Cover loosely with plastic wrap or a clean towel and let it rise again in a warm place for 30-45 minutes, or until visibly puffy.
Preheat your oven to 375°F (190°C) during the second rise.
Brush the top and sides of the risen Zopf generously with the beaten egg wash.
Bake for 35-40 minutes, or until golden brown and the internal temperature reaches 200-210°F (93-99°C). If it browns too quickly, you can loosely tent it with foil.
Transfer the Zopf to a wire rack to cool completely before slicing and serving.
tips: For an extra shiny crust, brush with egg wash again halfway through baking.
Ensure your milk is not too hot, as it can kill the yeast. It should feel comfortably warm to the touch.
Zopf is best enjoyed fresh, but leftovers can be lightly toasted or used for French toast.

spiced-ale.title: Spiced Ale (Wassail)
spiced-ale.intro: Spiced Ale, often known as Wassail, is a warming, festive drink traditionally enjoyed during the Twelve Days of Christmas, particularly on St. Stephen's Day (Boxing Day) and Twelfth Night. This ancient beverage, steeped in tradition, was used for toasting good health and a bountiful harvest in the coming year, often sung while going door-to-door or blessing orchards. It's a perfect comforting beverage for winter celebrations.
ingredients: 6 cups (1.4 liters) good quality brown ale or hard cider
2-3 small baking apples (such as Braeburn or Honeycrisp), cored
1/2 cup (100 grams) light brown sugar, packed, or to taste
1-inch (2.5 cm) piece fresh ginger, peeled and thinly sliced
1/2 teaspoon whole cloves (plus extra for studding apples/orange)
1 large orange, sliced or studded with cloves
steps: Preheat oven to 350°F (175°C). Stud the cored apples with a few whole cloves each. Place apples in a small baking dish with a splash of water and bake for 20-30 minutes, or until tender but not mushy.

In a large non-reactive pot or Dutch oven, combine the ale (or hard cider), brown sugar, cinnamon sticks, sliced ginger, and the 1/2 teaspoon of whole cloves. If not using clove-studded apples or orange, add more whole cloves directly to the pot.

Gently heat the mixture over medium-low heat, stirring occasionally, until the sugar dissolves and the ale is hot but not boiling. Do not allow it to boil, as this will cook off the alcohol and diminish the flavor.
Add the baked, clove-studded apples and orange slices (or clove-studded orange) to the pot. If using, stir in the brandy or sherry.
Continue to simmer gently for at least 15-20 minutes to allow the flavors to meld and deepen.
Taste and adjust sweetness if desired, adding more brown sugar if preferred.
Ladle the hot spiced ale into heatproof mugs or glasses. Serve with a baked apple in each mug, if desired, and a fresh cinnamon stick or orange slice for garnish.
tips: For a non-alcoholic version, use non-alcoholic apple cider or ginger ale instead of beer.
Traditional recipes sometimes call for 'lambswool' – roasted apple pulp mixed into the drink, which adds a frothy texture.
Experiment with different spices like star anise, allspice berries, or a bay leaf for varied flavor profiles.

panettone.title: Traditional Panettone
panettone.intro: Panettone is a classic Italian sweet bread, rich with eggs, butter, and candied fruits. It's a beloved symbol of Christmas, often enjoyed throughout the Advent season, particularly on the Fourth Sunday, and continues to be a festive treat well into the New Year, gracing tables on New Year's Day as a symbol of good fortune and celebration.
panettone.prepTime: 1 hour 30 min active (plus 10-14 hours passive rising)
ingredients: 3 large egg yolks, at room temperature
1 cup (226g) unsalted butter, very soft, cut into 1-inch (2.5 cm) pieces
1 Panettone paper mold, 7-inch (18 cm) diameter x 4.5-inch (11 cm) tall
steps: Prepare the fruits: In a small bowl, combine the golden raisins, candied orange peel, and rum or brandy. Let soak for at least 30 minutes, or preferably overnight, stirring occasionally. Drain well and pat dry before adding to the dough.

Make the preferment: In the bowl of a stand mixer, combine the warm milk, 1 teaspoon yeast, 1 teaspoon sugar, and 1/2 cup (60g) bread flour. Whisk until smooth. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm place for 30-60 minutes, until bubbly and foamy.

First Dough: To the preferment, add 1 cup (120g) of the remaining bread flour, 1/4 cup (50g) of the remaining granulated sugar, 1 whole egg, and 1 egg yolk. Attach the dough hook to your stand mixer and mix on low speed for 2 minutes, then increase to medium-low and knead for 8-10 minutes until the dough is smooth and elastic.
Transfer the dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let rise in a warm place for 2-3 hours, or until doubled in size.

Second Dough: Return the first dough to the stand mixer bowl. Add the remaining 2 1/2 cups (300g) bread flour, remaining 1/2 cup (100g) granulated sugar, remaining 1 1/4 teaspoons (4g) yeast, remaining 2 whole eggs, remaining 2 egg yolks, salt, vanilla extract, orange zest, and lemon zest. Mix on low speed for 5 minutes until combined, then increase to medium-low and knead for 10-15 minutes until the dough is very elastic and pulls away from the sides of the bowl.

With the mixer running on medium-low, add the softened butter, one piece at a time, allowing each piece to be fully incorporated before adding the next. This process will take 10-15 minutes. Continue kneading until the dough is very smooth, shiny, and passes the 'windowpane test' (you can stretch a small piece thin enough to see light through it without tearing).
Add the drained, dried fruits to the dough and mix on low speed for 1-2 minutes until evenly distributed.
Transfer the dough to a large, lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let rise in a warm place for 2-3 hours, or until nearly doubled in size.
Gently deflate the dough and turn it out onto a lightly floured surface. Shape it into a tight ball. Place the dough into the panettone paper mold.
Cover the mold loosely with plastic wrap or a clean kitchen towel and let it proof in a warm place for 3-5 hours, or until the dough has risen to the top edge of the mold and is visibly puffy.
Preheat your oven to 350°F (175°C). If desired, use a sharp knife or razor blade to cut a shallow 'X' on top of the panettone and place a small pat of butter in the center.
Bake for 45-55 minutes, or until the top is golden brown and a thermometer inserted into the center reads 195-200°F (90-93°C). If the top browns too quickly, loosely tent with foil.

Immediately upon removing from the oven, insert two long metal skewers horizontally through the base of the panettone, about 1 inch (2.5 cm) from the bottom, parallel to each other. Invert the panettone and hang it upside down (e.g., between two chairs or over a pot) for at least 4-6 hours, or overnight, to cool completely. This prevents the rich, airy crumb from collapsing.
Once completely cool, remove the skewers. Panettone is best enjoyed sliced and served at room temperature.
tips: A stand mixer with a dough hook is highly recommended for this recipe, as the dough is very rich and sticky.

Do not rush the rising times; proper fermentation is crucial for Panettone's characteristic flavor and texture. A slightly cooler rise (e.g., in the refrigerator overnight for the bulk fermentation) can further develop flavor.
Cooling the Panettone upside down is essential to maintain its tall, airy structure and prevent it from compacting under its own weight.

roasted-meat.title: Roasted Pork Loin with Apple and Sage
roasted-meat.intro: Twelfth Night, marking the end of the Christmas season and the eve of Epiphany, is a time for a final festive feast before the return to ordinary time. A succulent roasted pork loin, often served with seasonal fruits like apples and aromatic herbs, makes for a magnificent centerpiece, symbolizing abundance and celebration. This dish is a perfect way to gather family and friends for one last holiday indulgence.
ingredients: 1 (2-3 pound / 0.9-1.4 kg) boneless pork loin roast
2 medium apples, such as Honeycrisp or Fuji, cored and cut into 1-inch (2.5 cm) wedges
1 large onion, cut into 1-inch (2.5 cm) wedges
1/2 cup (120 ml) chicken or apple cider broth
steps: Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C).
Pat the pork loin dry with paper towels.
In a small bowl, combine olive oil, dried sage, dried thyme, salt, and black pepper. Rub the mixture all over the pork loin.
Place the pork loin in a roasting pan. Arrange the apple and onion wedges around the pork.
Pour the chicken or apple cider broth into the bottom of the roasting pan.
Roast for 60-90 minutes, or until an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of the pork reads 145°F (63°C).
Remove the pork from the oven, transfer it to a cutting board, and tent loosely with foil. Let it rest for 10-15 minutes before slicing.
While the pork rests, you can make a pan sauce from the drippings in the roasting pan, if desired, by simmering them on the stovetop.
Slice the pork into 1/2-inch (1.25 cm) thick rounds and serve with the roasted apples and onions, and any pan sauce.
tips: For extra flavor, score the fat cap of the pork loin in a crosshatch pattern before seasoning.
Resting the meat is crucial for juicy results; it allows the juices to redistribute throughout the roast.
Serve with roasted root vegetables or mashed potatoes for a complete festive meal.

lambs-lettuce-salad.title: Lamb's Lettuce Salad
lambs-lettuce-salad.intro: This delicate Lamb's Lettuce Salad, also known as Mâche, is a wonderful way to celebrate Candlemas, the Feast of the Presentation, which traditionally marks the midpoint of winter and the anticipation of spring. Its tender, slightly nutty leaves are among the first greens to emerge, symbolizing new life and the approaching warmth, making it a perfect fresh counterpoint to heartier winter fare.
ingredients: 3 tablespoons (45 ml) extra virgin olive oil
steps: Gently wash the lamb's lettuce under cool running water, ensuring all grit is removed.
Carefully dry the lettuce using a salad spinner or by patting it very gently with paper towels. It is crucial for the lettuce to be thoroughly dry for the dressing to adhere properly.
In a small bowl, whisk together the extra virgin olive oil, white wine vinegar, Dijon mustard, salt, and pepper until well combined and emulsified.
If using, stir the finely minced shallot into the dressing mixture.
Place the dried lamb's lettuce in a large salad bowl.
Just before serving, pour the prepared dressing over the lettuce.
Toss gently to coat all the delicate leaves evenly.
Serve immediately to enjoy the crisp texture and fresh flavor.
tips: For added texture and a complementary flavor, sprinkle the salad with a few toasted walnuts or pecans.
A touch of crumbled goat cheese or feta can also enhance the delicate taste of the mâche.
Always dress lamb's lettuce just before serving, as its tender leaves can wilt quickly once combined with dressing.

crepes-with-butter-and-sugar.title: Candlemas Crêpes with Butter and Sugar
crepes-with-butter-and-sugar.intro: These delicate crêpes are a beloved tradition for Candlemas, or La Chandeleur, celebrated on February 2nd. Their round, golden shape is said to symbolize the sun and the return of longer days after winter, bringing hopes of prosperity for the year ahead. Simple yet elegant, they are traditionally enjoyed with just a sprinkle of sugar and a touch of butter.
ingredients: 2 tablespoons (28g) unsalted butter, melted, plus more for cooking
steps: In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, salt, and 1 tablespoon of granulated sugar.
In a separate bowl, whisk the eggs and milk together until well combined.
Gradually add the wet ingredients to the dry ingredients, whisking constantly until the batter is smooth and free of lumps.
Stir in the 2 tablespoons of melted butter.
Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and let the batter rest in the refrigerator for at least 30 minutes, or up to 2 hours. This allows the flour to fully hydrate, resulting in more tender crêpes.
Heat a 8-inch (20 cm) non-stick crêpe pan or skillet over medium heat. Lightly butter the pan for the first crêpe.
Pour about 1/4 cup (60ml) of batter into the hot pan, immediately tilting and swirling the pan to coat the bottom evenly with a thin layer of batter.
Cook for 1-2 minutes, or until the edges are lightly golden and the crêpe easily lifts from the pan.
Flip the crêpe with a spatula and cook for another 30-60 seconds, until lightly browned on the second side.
Slide the cooked crêpe onto a plate. Repeat with the remaining batter, lightly buttering the pan as needed between crêpes.
To serve, spread a thin layer of softened butter on each warm crêpe, sprinkle generously with granulated sugar, and fold into quarters or roll up.
tips: Ensure your pan is hot enough; a drop of water should sizzle and evaporate quickly. If crêpes are sticking, the pan might not be hot enough or needs more butter.
For a richer flavor, you can add 1 teaspoon of vanilla extract or a tablespoon of rum to the batter.
Leftover crêpes can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 2 days, separated by parchment paper, and reheated gently in a pan or microwave.

ham-and-cheese-crepes.title: Ham and Cheese Crepes for Candlemas
ham-and-cheese-crepes.intro: Candlemas, or La Chandeleur, celebrated on February 2nd, marks the presentation of Jesus at the Temple and is traditionally associated with light and purification. In France, it's a beloved custom to make and eat crêpes on this day, symbolizing prosperity and the return of longer, sunnier days. Savory Ham and Cheese Crêpes are a classic choice, offering a comforting and delicious meal perfect for sharing with family.
ingredients: 2 tablespoons (28 g) unsalted butter, melted, plus more for cooking
1 1/2 cups (360 ml) whole milk, warmed (for béchamel)
Salt and freshly ground black pepper to taste
8 ounces (225 g) cooked ham, thinly sliced or diced
8 ounces (225 g) Gruyère or Emmental cheese, grated
steps: Prepare the Crêpe Batter: In a large bowl, whisk together the flour and salt. In a separate bowl, whisk the eggs and milk. Gradually add the wet ingredients to the dry ingredients, whisking until smooth. Stir in the 2 tablespoons of melted butter. Cover the bowl and let the batter rest in the refrigerator for at least 30 minutes, or up to 2 hours.

Make the Béchamel Sauce: While the batter rests, melt 2 tablespoons of butter in a medium saucepan over medium heat. Add the flour and whisk constantly for 1-2 minutes to create a roux. Gradually whisk in the warm milk, a little at a time, ensuring no lumps form. Continue to whisk until the sauce thickens to your desired consistency, about 5-7 minutes. Season with nutmeg (if using), salt, and pepper. Keep warm over very low heat, stirring occasionally, or set aside and gently reheat later.

Cook the Crêpes: Heat an 8-inch (20 cm) non-stick crêpe pan or skillet over medium heat. Lightly grease the pan with a small amount of melted butter. Pour about 1/4 cup (60 ml) of batter into the center of the hot pan, immediately tilting and swirling the pan to spread the batter evenly into a thin circle. Cook for 1-2 minutes until the edges are golden and the crêpe easily lifts. Flip and cook for another 30-60 seconds on the second side. Transfer the cooked crêpe to a plate and repeat with the remaining batter, stacking the crêpes as you go.

Assemble the Crêpes: Lay a cooked crêpe flat. Spread a thin layer of béchamel sauce over one half of the crêpe. Sprinkle a generous amount of grated cheese over the sauce, then top with some ham slices or diced ham.

Fold and Heat: Fold the crêpe in half, then in half again to form a triangle, or simply roll it up. You can serve them immediately, or for a warmer, melted cheese experience, place the assembled crêpes on a baking sheet. Bake in a preheated oven at 350°F (175°C) for 5-10 minutes, or until the cheese is melted and bubbly. Alternatively, heat them gently in a skillet.
Serve: Serve the warm Ham and Cheese Crêpes immediately, perhaps with a side salad.
tips: For extra flavor, add a pinch of dried herbs like chives or parsley to the béchamel sauce.
Ensure your crêpe batter is well-rested; this allows the flour to fully hydrate, resulting in more tender crêpes.
If you don't have a crêpe pan, a good quality non-stick skillet works perfectly.

cinnamon-atole.title: Cinnamon Atole
cinnamon-atole.intro: Cinnamon Atole is a warm, thick, and comforting beverage, often made from masa (corn dough) or masa harina, milk, and spices. It's a staple in Mexican cuisine, especially during colder months and festive occasions. On Candlemas (Día de la Candelaria) on February 2nd, it's traditionally served alongside tamales, marking the end of the Christmas season and the presentation of Jesus at the Temple.
ingredients: 1/2 cup (60 g) masa harina for tortillas
1/2 cup (100 g) piloncillo (Mexican brown sugar cone), chopped, or 1/2 cup (100 g) packed light brown sugar
2 cinnamon sticks (about 3 inches or 7.5 cm each)
steps: In a medium bowl, whisk together the masa harina with 1 cup (240 ml) of the milk until smooth and no lumps remain. Set aside.
In a large saucepan or pot, combine the remaining 3 cups (720 ml) milk, water, piloncillo (or brown sugar), cinnamon sticks, and salt.
Heat the mixture over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until the piloncillo or brown sugar has completely dissolved and the mixture is warm, but not boiling.
Slowly pour the masa harina mixture into the saucepan, whisking constantly to prevent lumps.

Continue to cook over medium-low heat, stirring frequently with a whisk or wooden spoon, for 15-20 minutes, or until the atole thickens to your desired consistency (it should be like a thin gravy or thick hot chocolate). Be careful not to let it scorch at the bottom.
Remove the cinnamon sticks. If using, stir in the vanilla extract.
Serve hot in mugs.
tips: For a thinner atole, add a little more milk or water until desired consistency is reached.
Atole can be made with various flavorings like chocolate (Champurrado), fruit purees, or nuts.
Always stir frequently while cooking to prevent lumps and sticking to the bottom of the pot.

dry-cider.title: Mulled Dry Cider for Candlemas
dry-cider.intro: On Candlemas, February 2nd, traditions often include enjoying crepes, especially in France. A perfect accompaniment to these delicate pancakes, or simply a warming treat for a cold winter's day, is a fragrant mulled dry cider. This recipe elevates a simple purchased dry cider into a comforting, spiced beverage, ideal for sharing during this festive and reflective holiday.
ingredients: 1/2 gallon (about 1.9 liters) dry apple cider (hard cider, not apple juice)
1/4 cup (60 ml) fresh orange juice (from about 1/2 orange)
2 tablespoons (30 ml) maple syrup or honey, or to taste (optional)
1/4 cup (60 ml) brandy or Calvados (optional, for an adult version)
steps: Pour the dry apple cider into a large saucepan or pot.
Add the cinnamon sticks, whole cloves, star anise pods, and fresh orange juice to the cider. If using, add maple syrup or honey now.
Heat the mixture over medium heat, bringing it to a gentle simmer. Do not boil, as boiling can cause the alcohol to evaporate and can diminish the delicate flavors of the spices.
Reduce the heat to low and let the cider gently simmer for 15-20 minutes, allowing the flavors to meld and deepen.
Taste the mulled cider and adjust sweetness if desired, adding more maple syrup or honey if preferred.
If making an adult version, stir in the brandy or Calvados just before serving.
Strain the cider through a fine-mesh sieve to remove the whole spices, or leave them in for presentation.
Ladle the warm mulled cider into heatproof mugs or glasses. Garnish each serving with an orange slice, if desired.
tips: For a spicier kick, add a few slices of fresh ginger or a pinch of ground nutmeg to the simmering cider.
If you prefer a less dry cider, you can use a semi-dry or even a traditional hard cider and adjust the sweetener accordingly.
Leftover mulled cider can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 3 days and gently reheated on the stovetop or in the microwave.

foamy-champurrado.title: Foamy Champurrado
events: Feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe
foamy-champurrado.intro: Champurrado is a warm, thick, and comforting chocolate-based atole, traditionally enjoyed in Mexico during cooler months and especially for festive occasions. It's a beloved beverage for the Feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe on December 12th, and a staple for Candlemas (Día de la Candelaria) on February 2nd, where it's often served alongside tamales, symbolizing warmth and community during these significant celebrations.
ingredients: 1 (3.5 oz / 100 g) piloncillo cone, or 1/2 cup (100 g) dark brown sugar
1 (3.5 oz / 100 g) Mexican chocolate tablet, chopped
steps: In a large saucepan, combine the water, piloncillo (or brown sugar), and cinnamon stick. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring occasionally until the piloncillo is completely dissolved.
Add the chopped Mexican chocolate to the simmering mixture, stirring until it is fully melted and incorporated.
In a separate bowl, whisk together the masa harina with 1 cup (240 ml) of the whole milk until smooth and no lumps remain.
Gradually whisk the masa harina mixture into the chocolate mixture in the saucepan.
Add the remaining 3 cups (720 ml) of whole milk and the salt to the saucepan.

Continue to cook over medium-low heat, stirring constantly with a whisk or a molinillo (a traditional Mexican whisk) to prevent sticking and to create foam, until the champurrado thickens to your desired consistency, about 15-20 minutes. Do not boil.
Remove the cinnamon stick. Stir in the vanilla extract, if using.
For extra foam, vigorously whisk the champurrado just before serving, or use a molinillo.
Serve hot in mugs.
tips: For a richer flavor, toast the masa harina lightly in a dry pan before mixing with milk.
Adjust the sweetness by adding more piloncillo or sugar to taste.
If the champurrado becomes too thick, thin it with a little more milk or water.

figgy-pudding.title: Figgy Pudding
figgy-pudding.intro: Figgy Pudding, a rich, steamed dessert laden with dried fruit and spices, is a quintessential part of traditional British Christmas celebrations. Serving it on Twelfth Night marks the grand finale of the festive season, a sweet and warming conclusion to the revelry before the decorations come down. Its historical roots are deep, often associated with carols and merriment.
ingredients: 1 cup (150g) dried figs, stems removed and finely chopped
1/2 cup (120ml) brandy or strong black tea
1/2 cup (100g) shredded suet (or cold butter, grated)
For serving: Brandy butter or custard
steps: In a small bowl, combine the chopped dried figs with the brandy or strong black tea. Let them soak for at least 30 minutes, or preferably longer, to plump up.
In a large mixing bowl, combine the breadcrumbs, flour, dark brown sugar, shredded suet, cinnamon, nutmeg, cloves, allspice, salt, and orange zest. Mix well to combine all dry ingredients.
Add the soaked figs (and any remaining liquid), the lightly beaten eggs, and the milk to the dry ingredients. Mix thoroughly until everything is well combined into a thick batter.
Generously grease a 1.5-quart (1.5L) pudding basin with butter. Spoon the pudding mixture into the prepared basin, pressing it down gently to remove any air pockets.

Cut a circle of parchment paper slightly larger than the top of the basin and grease one side. Place it greased-side down over the pudding. Then, cover the basin tightly with aluminum foil, crimping it securely around the rim. You can also tie it with kitchen twine for extra security.

Place the pudding basin on a trivet or a heatproof plate in a large pot. Pour boiling water into the pot until it comes halfway up the sides of the pudding basin. Bring the water to a gentle simmer, then cover the pot tightly.

Steam the pudding for 3 to 3.5 hours, checking the water level periodically and topping up with more boiling water if needed. The pudding is done when a skewer inserted into the center comes out clean.
Carefully remove the pudding basin from the pot. Let it cool for 10-15 minutes before inverting it onto a serving plate. Serve warm with brandy butter, custard, or a dollop of whipped cream.
tips: This pudding can be made several days or even weeks in advance. Once cooled, wrap it tightly in plastic wrap and foil, and store in a cool, dark place. Reheat by steaming for 1-2 hours.
For a non-alcoholic version, replace the brandy with orange juice, apple juice, or strong black tea for soaking the figs and in the batter.
To serve flambéed, warm a few tablespoons of brandy in a small saucepan, ignite carefully, and pour over the pudding just before serving.

oaxacan-tamales.title: Oaxacan Tamales
oaxacan-tamales.intro: Oaxacan tamales, distinguished by their banana leaf wrapping, offer a unique aroma and moist texture, making them a festive favorite. They are a central dish for Día de la Candelaria (Candlemas) on February 2nd in Mexico, a day when families gather to enjoy tamales, often hosted by whoever found the baby Jesus figurine in the Rosca de Reyes.
ingredients: 2 pounds (900 g) masa harina for tamales (not instant masa for tortillas)
1.5 cups (340 g) lard or vegetable shortening, softened
4 cups (960 ml) warm chicken broth, plus more if needed
2 pounds (900 g) pork shoulder, cut into 2-inch (5 cm) chunks
8-10 dried Guajillo chiles, stems and seeds removed
3-4 dried Ancho chiles, stems and seeds removed
1/2 cup (120 ml) reserved pork cooking broth
1 (16-ounce / 450 g) package banana leaves, thawed if frozen, cut into 8x8 inch (20x20 cm) squares
steps: Prepare Pork Filling: Place pork shoulder, 1/2 onion (quartered), 3 cloves garlic, and 1 teaspoon salt in a large pot. Cover with water. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer for 1 to 1.5 hours, or until pork is very tender. Reserve 1/2 cup (120 ml) of the cooking broth. Shred the cooked pork with two forks.

Prepare Red Chile Sauce: While pork cooks, toast the dried chiles in a dry skillet over medium heat for 30 seconds per side until fragrant (do not burn). Place toasted chiles in a bowl, cover with hot water, and let soak for 20-30 minutes until softened.

Drain the softened chiles, reserving some soaking liquid. Blend the chiles with 1/2 chopped onion, 3 cloves garlic, cumin, oregano, and 1/2 cup (120 ml) reserved pork broth until very smooth. Add a splash of chile soaking liquid if needed to help blend.

Strain the chile sauce through a fine-mesh sieve into a saucepan to remove any skin or seeds. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring occasionally, for 10-15 minutes until slightly thickened. Season with salt to taste.
Combine the shredded pork with enough red chile sauce to coat it well (you may not use all the sauce). Set aside.
Prepare Banana Leaves: If using banana leaves, gently pass each leaf square over an open flame or hot skillet for a few seconds until pliable. This prevents cracking.
Prepare Masa: In a large bowl or stand mixer with a paddle attachment, beat the softened lard (or shortening) until light and fluffy, about 5 minutes.

In a separate bowl, whisk together the masa harina, 2 teaspoons salt, and baking powder. Gradually add the masa harina mixture to the beaten lard, alternating with warm chicken broth, mixing until a soft, spreadable dough forms. The masa should be light and fluffy. To test if it's ready, drop a small piece into a glass of cold water; if it floats, it's ready. If not, beat for a few more minutes and retest.
Assemble Tamales: Lay a banana leaf square flat with the smooth side up. Spread about 1/4 cup (60 ml) of masa evenly over the center of the leaf, leaving a border.
Place 1-2 tablespoons of the pork filling in the center of the masa.
Fold one long side of the banana leaf over the filling, then fold the other long side to overlap. Fold up the bottom and top ends to create a neat packet.

Steam Tamales: Place a steamer basket in a large pot with about 2 inches (5 cm) of water, ensuring the water does not touch the basket. Arrange the tamales upright or stacked, but not too tightly, in the steamer.
Bring the water to a boil, then reduce heat to medium-low, cover tightly, and steam for 1 to 1.5 hours.
Check for Doneness: Tamales are done when the masa easily separates from the banana leaf. If it sticks, steam for another 15-20 minutes and recheck.
Let the tamales rest for 10-15 minutes after steaming before serving.
tips: For an authentic touch, add a small piece of avocado leaf to each tamale before folding.
Cooked tamales can be frozen for up to 3 months. Reheat by steaming for 20-30 minutes or microwaving until hot.
Vary the filling with shredded chicken in green salsa (salsa verde) or cheese with jalapeños for different options.

candlemas-bread.title: Candlemas Bread
candlemas-bread.intro: Candlemas Bread is a traditional sweet, enriched yeast bread often baked to celebrate Candlemas, also known as the Feast of the Presentation of Jesus at the Temple, on February 2nd. This day marks the end of the Christmas season and is associated with the blessing of candles, symbolizing Christ as the Light of the World, and this bread often represents warmth and light in the home.
ingredients: 1 cup (240 ml) whole milk, warmed to 105-115°F (40-46°C)
2 1/4 teaspoons (7g) active dry yeast (1 standard packet)
1/4 cup (57g) unsalted butter, melted and cooled slightly
3 1/2 to 4 cups (420-480g) all-purpose flour, plus more for dusting
1 tablespoon (15 ml) water or milk, for egg wash
steps: In a large bowl, combine the warm milk and 1 teaspoon of granulated sugar. Sprinkle the yeast over the top and let it sit for 5-10 minutes until foamy, indicating the yeast is active.
Add the remaining 1/4 cup (50g) granulated sugar, salt, the first large egg, melted butter, and lemon zest (if using) to the yeast mixture. Whisk until well combined.

Gradually add 3 1/2 cups (420g) of the flour, mixing with a wooden spoon or dough hook until a shaggy dough forms. If the dough is too sticky, add the remaining flour 1/4 cup (30g) at a time until it pulls away from the sides of the bowl.
Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and knead for 8-10 minutes, until it is smooth and elastic. Alternatively, use a stand mixer with a dough hook for 6-8 minutes.

Lightly grease a clean large bowl. Place the dough in the bowl, turning once to coat. Cover the bowl with plastic wrap or a clean kitchen towel and let it rise in a warm place for 1 to 1 1/2 hours, or until doubled in size.
Once doubled, gently punch down the dough to release the air. Turn it out onto a lightly floured surface.

Shape the dough into a round loaf or a braided loaf. For a round loaf, simply tuck the edges under to form a smooth ball. For a braid, divide the dough into three equal pieces, roll each into a long rope, and braid them together, pinching the ends to seal.

Place the shaped dough on a baking sheet lined with parchment paper. Cover loosely with plastic wrap or a clean towel and let it rise again in a warm place for 30-45 minutes, or until noticeably puffy.
Preheat your oven to 375°F (190°C). In a small bowl, whisk together the second large egg and 1 tablespoon of water or milk to create an egg wash.
Brush the top and sides of the risen bread with the egg wash. This will give it a beautiful golden crust.
Bake for 30-35 minutes, or until the bread is golden brown and sounds hollow when tapped on the bottom. An instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should register 200-210°F (93-99°C).
Transfer the bread to a wire rack to cool completely before slicing and serving.
tips: For extra shine, brush the bread with a little melted butter immediately after it comes out of the oven.
You can add 1/2 cup (75g) of golden raisins or dried cranberries to the dough during the last minute of kneading for a fruitier bread.
Serve this bread warm with butter, jam, or honey for a comforting treat on Candlemas.

mulled-wine.title: Traditional Mulled Wine (Glühwein)
mulled-wine.intro: Mulled Wine, known as Glühwein in German-speaking regions, is a quintessential warm beverage enjoyed during the colder months, perfectly suited for festive gatherings like St. Martin's Day (Martinstag) and the wild Perchtenlauf of Perchta Day. Its aromatic spices and comforting warmth provide a welcome respite from the chill, fostering a sense of community and celebration as winter approaches.
ingredients: 2 (750 ml) bottles dry red wine (such as Merlot or Cabernet Sauvignon)
1/4 cup (50 g) granulated sugar, or to taste
1/4 cup (60 ml) water (optional, for dissolving sugar)
steps: Combine the orange slices, cinnamon sticks, whole cloves, star anise pods, and sugar in a large non-reactive pot or Dutch oven.
If using, add the 1/4 cup of water to the pot. Heat over medium-low heat, stirring occasionally, until the sugar has dissolved and the spices become fragrant, about 5 minutes.
Pour in both bottles of red wine and the brandy or cognac (if using). Stir gently to combine.

Heat the mixture over low to medium heat, ensuring it warms through but does not boil. Boiling will cause the alcohol to evaporate and can make the wine taste bitter. Aim for a gentle simmer, just before boiling, for about 15-20 minutes.
Once heated, remove the pot from the heat. You can either strain out the spices and orange slices for a smoother drink or leave them in for presentation and continued flavor infusion.
Ladle the warm mulled wine into heatproof mugs or glasses and serve immediately.
tips: Do not boil the mulled wine; gentle heating is key to preserving the alcohol and flavor.
Adjust the sweetness to your preference by adding more sugar, or for a less sweet version, omit the sugar entirely.
For an extra citrusy kick, add a few strips of lemon peel along with the orange slices.

sweet-tamales.title: Sweet Tamales for Candlemas
sweet-tamales.intro: Candlemas, or Día de la Candelaria, on February 2nd, marks the presentation of Jesus at the Temple and the purification of the Virgin Mary. In Mexico, it's a beloved tradition to celebrate with tamales, often hosted by the person who found the baby Jesus figurine in the Rosca de Reyes on Epiphany. Sweet tamales, with their delightful hint of sugar and fruit, are a festive and comforting way to honor this day, bringing warmth and community to the winter celebration.
ingredients: 1 cup (225g) lard or vegetable shortening, at room temperature
2 cups (480ml) warm water or milk, plus more if needed
steps: Place corn husks in a large bowl or pot, cover with very hot water, and weigh down with a plate to keep them submerged. Let them soak for at least 30 minutes, or until pliable. Drain and pat dry before using.
In a large mixing bowl, using an electric mixer, beat the lard or shortening until light and fluffy, about 3-5 minutes.
Gradually add the granulated sugar to the lard, beating until well combined and fluffy, about 2-3 minutes more.
In a separate bowl, whisk together the masa harina, baking powder, salt, and ground cinnamon.
Gradually add the dry masa mixture to the creamed lard mixture, alternating with the warm water or milk, beginning and ending with the masa mixture. Add the vanilla extract.

Continue beating the masa dough for about 10-15 minutes, until it is very light, fluffy, and resembles a thick cake batter. To test if it's ready, drop a small 1/2 teaspoon of dough into a glass of cold water; if it floats, it's ready. If it sinks, continue beating for a few more minutes and retest.

To assemble the tamales, take one softened corn husk, place it with the wider end at the top. Spread about 2-3 tablespoons of masa dough evenly over the wider part of the husk, leaving about 1 inch (2.5 cm) clear at the top and sides.
If using, sprinkle a small amount of raisins down the center of the masa.
Fold one long side of the husk over the filling, then fold the other long side over to overlap. Fold the narrow bottom end of the husk up towards the center. Leave the top open.
Repeat with the remaining masa and corn husks.

Arrange the tamales upright (open-end up) in a steamer basket. If you don't have a steamer, you can use a large pot with a colander or a metal rack at the bottom, ensuring the water level is below the tamales.
Pour about 2-3 inches (5-7.5 cm) of water into the bottom of the steamer or pot. Bring the water to a boil, then reduce heat to a steady simmer. Cover tightly with a lid.
Steam the tamales for 1 hour to 1 hour 15 minutes, or until the masa easily separates from the corn husk. You may need to add more hot water to the pot during steaming if it evaporates too quickly.
Carefully remove tamales from the steamer and let them rest for 5-10 minutes before serving. This allows them to firm up slightly.
tips: For an extra fruity flavor, you can add 1/4 cup (60g) of finely diced candied fruit or finely chopped dried pineapple to the masa dough.
Ensure your masa dough is very light and fluffy; this is key to tender tamales. The 'float test' is a reliable indicator.
Tamales can be made ahead of time and refrigerated for up to 3 days or frozen for up to 2 months. Reheat by steaming or microwaving until warmed through.

dumplings.title: Chinese Pork and Cabbage Dumplings (Jiaozi)
dumplings.intro: These savory dumplings, known as Jiaozi, are a cornerstone of Lunar New Year celebrations (Chunjie), symbolizing wealth and prosperity due to their shape resembling ancient gold ingots. Families gather to make and enjoy them, fostering togetherness and good fortune for the coming year. While not traditionally associated with Perchta Day (Perchtenlauf), their hearty and comforting nature makes them a perfect, warming meal for any cold winter festival.
ingredients: 2 cups (240g) all-purpose flour, plus more for dusting
1 pound (450g) ground pork (medium fat content is best)
2 cups (about 1/2 small head) finely chopped napa cabbage
steps: Prepare the Dough: In a large bowl, combine flour and salt. Gradually add warm water, mixing until a shaggy dough forms. Knead on a lightly floured surface for 5-7 minutes until smooth and elastic. Cover with plastic wrap and let rest for at least 30 minutes at room temperature.

Prepare the Cabbage: Place the finely chopped napa cabbage in a bowl. Sprinkle with 1/2 teaspoon of salt and let sit for 10 minutes. Squeeze out as much excess water as possible from the cabbage using your hands or a clean kitchen towel. This prevents the filling from becoming watery.

Make the Filling: In a large bowl, combine the ground pork, squeezed cabbage, green onions, grated ginger, minced garlic, soy sauce, sesame oil, and white pepper. Mix thoroughly with your hands or a spoon until all ingredients are well combined and slightly sticky.

Form the Wrappers: Divide the rested dough into two equal portions. Roll one portion into a long log (about 1 inch / 2.5 cm diameter). Cut the log into 20-25 equal pieces. Flatten each piece into a small disc. On a lightly floured surface, roll each disc into a thin, round wrapper (about 3-4 inches / 7-10 cm in diameter), keeping the edges slightly thinner than the center. Repeat with the second dough portion.

Fill and Fold the Dumplings: Hold a wrapper in the palm of your hand. Place about 1 tablespoon of filling in the center. Moisten half of the wrapper edge with a little water. Fold the wrapper in half to create a crescent shape. Pinch the center closed, then make small pleats along one side of the wrapper, pressing them firmly against the other side to seal completely. Ensure no air is trapped inside. Place finished dumplings on a lightly floured baking sheet, making sure they don't touch.

Cook the Dumplings (Boiling Method): Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Carefully add 10-15 dumplings, ensuring not to overcrowd the pot. Stir gently to prevent sticking. Once the water returns to a boil, add about 1/2 cup (120ml) cold water. Repeat this process two more times. The dumplings are cooked when they float to the surface and appear plump (about 8-10 minutes total). Remove with a slotted spoon.

Cook the Dumplings (Pan-Frying/Potsticker Method): Heat 1-2 tablespoons of vegetable oil in a large non-stick skillet over medium-high heat. Place dumplings in a single layer, flat side down, and cook for 2-3 minutes until the bottoms are golden brown. Add about 1/2 cup (120ml) of water to the skillet, immediately cover with a lid, and steam for 5-7 minutes, or until the water has evaporated and the dumplings are cooked through. Remove the lid and cook for another minute to crisp the bottoms.
Prepare the Dipping Sauce: In a small bowl, whisk together soy sauce, rice vinegar, and sesame oil. Add chili oil to taste, if desired.
Serve: Serve the hot dumplings immediately with the dipping sauce.
tips: Freezing Dumplings: Uncooked dumplings can be frozen. Place them on a floured baking sheet and freeze until solid, then transfer to an airtight freezer bag. Cook from frozen, adding a few extra minutes to the cooking time.
Filling Variations: Experiment with different fillings! You can substitute ground chicken or shrimp, or add finely chopped mushrooms, carrots, or bok choy for more flavor and texture.
Perfect Pleats: Don't worry if your first few dumplings aren't perfect. Practice makes perfect! The key is to ensure a tight seal to keep the delicious filling inside.

milky-punch.title: Warming Milky Punch
milky-punch.intro: This comforting and rich Milky Punch is a perfect beverage to warm up with after witnessing the spirited Perchtenlauf on Perchta Day. Traditionally served in Alpine regions during the cold winter months, this sweet and spiced milk drink offers a soothing contrast to the wild energy of the Perchten, bringing a sense of warmth and festive cheer to the Epiphany celebrations.
ingredients: 1/2 cup (100 g) granulated sugar, or to taste
1 vanilla bean, split lengthwise, or 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
1/4 teaspoon freshly grated nutmeg, plus more for garnish
1/2 cup (120 ml) dark rum or brandy (optional)
steps: In a medium saucepan, combine the whole milk, granulated sugar, split vanilla bean (if using), cinnamon sticks, and 1/4 teaspoon freshly grated nutmeg.
Heat the mixture over medium-low heat, stirring occasionally, until the sugar is fully dissolved and the milk is hot but not boiling. Do not let it come to a rolling boil.

Once hot, remove the saucepan from the heat. If using a vanilla bean, scrape the seeds into the milk and discard the pod, or leave it in to infuse further. Let the mixture steep for 5-10 minutes to allow the flavors to meld.
Remove the cinnamon sticks from the milk.
If adding alcohol, stir in the dark rum or brandy now.
Pour the Milky Punch into heatproof mugs or glasses.
Garnish each serving with an additional sprinkle of freshly grated nutmeg before serving warm.
tips: For a non-alcoholic version suitable for all ages, simply omit the rum or brandy. The punch is delicious on its own.
Experiment with other spices like a few cloves or a star anise added to the milk while heating for a different aromatic profile.
To keep the punch warm for a gathering, transfer it to a slow cooker set on the 'warm' setting after removing the spices.

galette-des-rois.title: Galette des Rois
galette-des-rois.intro: The Galette des Rois, or 'King's Cake,' is a beloved French tradition enjoyed throughout January to celebrate Epiphany, or Three Kings Day. This flaky puff pastry cake, filled with a rich almond cream (frangipane), conceals a small charm called a 'fève,' and whoever finds it is crowned king or queen for the day, bringing good fortune.
ingredients: 1/2 teaspoon (2.5 ml) almond extract (or 1 tablespoon / 15 ml dark rum)
2 sheets (from a 14-ounce / 400 g package) store-bought puff pastry, thawed
1 fève (small ceramic charm or a whole almond)
steps: In a medium bowl, cream together the softened butter and granulated sugar until light and fluffy.
Beat in the 2 large eggs one at a time, ensuring each is fully incorporated before adding the next.
Stir in the almond flour, almond extract (or rum), and a pinch of salt until just combined to form the frangipane filling.
Lightly flour a clean surface and roll out each puff pastry sheet slightly to about a 10-inch (25 cm) circle.
Place one pastry circle on a parchment-lined baking sheet.
Spread the frangipane mixture evenly over the pastry circle, leaving a 1-inch (2.5 cm) border around the edge.
Carefully place the fève somewhere within the frangipane, ensuring it's fully covered.
Lightly moisten the exposed pastry border with a little water.
Place the second pastry circle directly on top of the first, aligning the edges.
Press down firmly around the edges to seal the two pastry circles together, then crimp with a fork for a decorative finish.
In a small bowl, whisk the egg yolk with 1 tablespoon (15 ml) of water or milk to create an egg wash.
Brush the top of the galette generously with the egg wash, being careful not to let it drip down the sides (this can prevent the pastry from rising).
Using the tip of a sharp knife, gently score a decorative pattern onto the top of the galette, such as spirals or a sunburst, without cutting through the pastry.
Chill the galette in the refrigerator for at least 30 minutes to firm up the pastry and frangipane.
Preheat your oven to 375°F (190°C).
Bake for 30 minutes, then reduce the oven temperature to 350°F (175°C) and continue baking for another 10-15 minutes, or until the galette is deeply golden brown and puffed.
Let the galette cool on the baking sheet for at least 15-20 minutes before slicing and serving warm.
tips: For an extra shine, you can brush the warm galette with a thin layer of apricot jam (warmed and strained) immediately after it comes out of the oven.
Ensure your puff pastry is very cold before baking; this helps achieve maximum puff and flakiness.
Traditionally, the youngest person at the table sits under the table and calls out who receives each slice, ensuring fairness in finding the fève.

hot-chocolate.title: Traditional Holiday Hot Chocolate
hot-chocolate.intro: This rich, velvety hot chocolate is a comforting embrace during the festive season. It's a beloved accompaniment to the Rosca de Reyes on Epiphany (Three Kings Day) in many Spanish-speaking countries, and a warm treat for the Feast of the Immaculate Conception (Immaculada). Its luxurious texture also makes it a perfect, cozy indulgence for special evenings, perhaps while enjoying a classic like Mozart's Magic Flute.
ingredients: 1/2 cup (120 ml) heavy cream (optional, for extra richness)
1/4 cup (50 g) granulated sugar, or to taste
4 ounces (113 g) good quality dark chocolate (70% cacao or higher), finely chopped
1 tablespoon (8 g) cornstarch, dissolved in 2 tablespoons (30 ml) cold milk (for thicker hot chocolate)
steps: In a medium saucepan, whisk together the cocoa powder, sugar, and salt.
Gradually whisk in 1 cup (240 ml) of the whole milk until smooth, forming a paste to prevent lumps.
Add the remaining 3 cups (720 ml) whole milk and heavy cream (if using) to the saucepan. Add the cinnamon stick, if using.
Heat over medium heat, whisking frequently, until the mixture is hot and just begins to simmer. Do not boil.
Remove the cinnamon stick. Add the chopped dark chocolate and continue to whisk until the chocolate is completely melted and the mixture is smooth.
If you desire a thicker hot chocolate, whisk in the dissolved cornstarch mixture. Continue to cook, whisking constantly, for 1-2 minutes until the hot chocolate thickens to your desired consistency.
Remove from heat and stir in the vanilla extract.
Pour into mugs and serve immediately.
tips: For an extra frothy hot chocolate, use an immersion blender or a milk frother just before serving.
Garnish with whipped cream, a sprinkle of cinnamon, or chocolate shavings for an even more festive touch.
Adjust the amount of sugar and dark chocolate to your preference for sweetness and intensity.

hot-mulled-cider.title: Hot Mulled Cider for Wassail
hot-mulled-cider.intro: This warming Hot Mulled Cider is a quintessential beverage for Old Twelfth Night Wassail, a traditional English custom to bless apple orchards and ensure a good harvest. Served steaming hot, it's perfect for toasting good health and prosperity during the mid-winter festivities, bringing cheer and comfort to all gathered.
ingredients: 1 gallon (3.8 L) apple cider, unfiltered preferred
1/4 cup (60 ml) maple syrup or brown sugar (optional, to taste)
1/2 cup (120 ml) brandy or dark rum (optional, for adult versions)
steps: Pour the apple cider into a large, non-reactive pot or Dutch oven.
Add the orange slices, cinnamon sticks, whole cloves, allspice berries, and star anise pods to the cider.
If using, stir in the maple syrup or brown sugar until dissolved.
Heat the mixture over medium heat until it just begins to simmer. Do not boil, as this can diminish the flavor of the spices.
Reduce the heat to low, cover, and let the cider gently simmer for at least 20 minutes to allow the flavors to meld and deepen.
Before serving, if desired, stir in the brandy or dark rum.
Strain the cider through a fine-mesh sieve to remove the spices and orange slices, or leave them in for presentation.
Serve hot in mugs, garnished with a fresh orange slice or cinnamon stick if desired.
tips: For a stronger spice flavor, gently crush the whole spices slightly before adding them to the cider.
This mulled cider can be kept warm in a slow cooker on the 'warm' setting for several hours, perfect for extended celebrations.
Adjust the sweetness to your liking; taste before adding any sweetener, as cider sweetness varies.

krapfen.title: Traditional Austrian Krapfen
krapfen.intro: Krapfen are delightful, fluffy doughnuts, often filled with apricot jam, that hold a special place in Alpine winter traditions. They are a beloved treat during the Rauhnächte (the twelve nights between Christmas and Epiphany) and especially for Perchta Day (Perchtenlauf), symbolizing abundance and warding off evil spirits as the community celebrates the transition from winter to the promise of spring.
ingredients: 1/4 cup (50 g) granulated sugar, plus 1 teaspoon
3 1/2 cups (420 g) all-purpose flour, plus more for dusting
1/4 cup (55 g) unsalted butter, melted and cooled
1/4 cup (60 ml) rum (optional, for flavor and to reduce oil absorption)
2 cups (480 g) apricot jam, strained if desired
4-6 cups (1-1.5 liters) vegetable oil or lard, for deep frying
1/2 cup (60 g) powdered sugar, for dusting
steps: In a small bowl, combine the lukewarm milk, 1 teaspoon of granulated sugar, and active dry yeast. Stir gently and let it sit for 5-10 minutes until foamy, indicating the yeast is active.
In a large mixing bowl, combine the flour, remaining 1/4 cup granulated sugar, and salt. Make a well in the center.
Pour the activated yeast mixture into the well. Add the egg yolks, whole egg, melted butter, vanilla extract, lemon zest (if using), and rum (if using).

Mix with a wooden spoon or a stand mixer with a dough hook until a shaggy dough forms. Knead for 8-10 minutes until the dough is smooth, elastic, and no longer sticky. It should pull away from the sides of the bowl.

Lightly grease a clean bowl, place the dough in it, turning once to coat. Cover with plastic wrap or a clean kitchen towel and let it rise in a warm place for 1 to 1.5 hours, or until doubled in size.
Once risen, gently punch down the dough and turn it out onto a lightly floured surface. Roll the dough to about 1/2 inch (1.25 cm) thickness.
Using a 3-inch (7.5 cm) round cutter, cut out circles. Gather the scraps, gently re-knead once, and cut out more circles. You should get 12-15 Krapfen.

Place the cut Krapfen on a lightly floured baking sheet, leaving some space between them. Cover loosely with a clean kitchen towel and let them rise again in a warm place for 30-45 minutes, or until visibly puffy.

While the Krapfen are rising for the second time, heat the vegetable oil or lard in a large heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven to 340-350°F (170-175°C). Use a deep-fry thermometer to monitor the temperature.

Carefully place 2-3 Krapfen at a time into the hot oil, ensuring not to overcrowd the pot. Fry for 2-3 minutes per side, until golden brown and puffed. The Krapfen should develop a light ring around the middle.
Using a slotted spoon, remove the fried Krapfen and place them on a wire rack lined with paper towels to drain excess oil.

Once slightly cooled but still warm, fill the Krapfen. You can do this by making a small incision on the side with a knife and piping in the apricot jam using a pastry bag fitted with a plain round tip, or by using a Bismark doughnut tip.
Dust generously with powdered sugar before serving. Krapfen are best enjoyed fresh.
tips: For the classic 'white ring' around the Krapfen, ensure your oil temperature is consistent and not too hot. Covering the pot for the first minute of frying can also help create steam for a better rise.
If you don't have a pastry bag, you can slice the Krapfen almost in half horizontally and spoon in the jam.
Experiment with other fillings like plum butter (Powidl) or vanilla cream for a delicious variation.

rosca-de-reyes.title: Rosca de Reyes (Three Kings' Bread)
rosca-de-reyes.intro: Rosca de Reyes is a sweet, brioche-like bread shaped into a ring and traditionally enjoyed on January 6th to celebrate Epiphany, or Three Kings' Day. This festive bread symbolizes the crown of the Three Wise Men, adorned with candied fruits representing jewels, and often hides a small figurine of the baby Jesus, representing the hiding of the infant from King Herod.
ingredients: 3 1/2 cups (420g) all-purpose flour, plus more for dusting
Assorted candied fruits (such as cherries, orange peel, figs)
steps: In a small bowl, combine the warm milk, 1 teaspoon of the granulated sugar, and the active dry yeast. Stir gently and let it sit for 5-10 minutes until foamy.
In a large bowl or the bowl of a stand mixer, combine the flour, remaining granulated sugar, and salt. Make a well in the center.
Pour the yeast mixture into the well. Add the eggs, softened butter, orange zest, and orange blossom water (if using).

Mix with a wooden spoon or the dough hook of a stand mixer on low speed until a shaggy dough forms. Increase speed to medium-low and knead for 8-10 minutes until the dough is smooth, elastic, and pulls away from the sides of the bowl. It will be slightly sticky.

Lightly grease a large bowl. Place the dough in the bowl, turning once to coat. Cover with plastic wrap or a clean kitchen towel and let rise in a warm place for 1.5 to 2 hours, or until doubled in size.

Punch down the dough gently. On a lightly floured surface, shape the dough into a long rope, then form it into a large ring, sealing the ends together. You can also place a greased, oven-safe ramekin or foil ball in the center of a baking sheet to help maintain the hole.
Carefully insert the small plastic baby figurine into the underside of the dough ring, making sure it's fully hidden.
Transfer the dough ring to a parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover loosely with plastic wrap or a towel and let rise again in a warm place for 45-60 minutes, or until noticeably puffy.

While the dough is rising for the second time, prepare the sugar paste topping: In a small bowl, cream together the softened butter and powdered sugar until light and fluffy. Gradually mix in the flour until a smooth paste forms.
Preheat your oven to 350°F (175°C).

Brush the risen dough with the beaten egg wash. Divide the sugar paste into several portions and flatten them into strips or shapes. Arrange these strips and the candied fruits decoratively on top of the dough. Sprinkle with granulated sugar.
Bake for 25-30 minutes, or until the Rosca de Reyes is golden brown and sounds hollow when tapped on the bottom. If it browns too quickly, you can loosely tent it with foil.
Let cool completely on a wire rack before slicing and serving. Be sure to warn guests about the hidden figurine!
tips: For a richer flavor, you can substitute some of the milk with orange juice.
If you don't have orange blossom water, you can omit it or add a few drops of vanilla extract for a different aroma.
The person who finds the baby figurine in their slice is traditionally said to host the next celebration, often a tamale party on Candelaria (Candlemas) on February 2nd.

blue-cheese.title: Blue Cheese and Walnut Tart
blue-cheese.intro: A savory tart, especially one featuring robust blue cheese and earthy walnuts, makes a wonderful addition to an Old Twelfth Night Wassail. It offers a rich, comforting counterpoint to the traditional spiced cider or ale, perfect for sharing during festive midwinter gatherings.
ingredients: 1 (9-inch/23 cm) unbaked pie crust (store-bought or homemade shortcrust pastry)
4 ounces (115 g) blue cheese (such as Stilton, Roquefort, or Gorgonzola), crumbled
steps: Preheat your oven to 375°F (190°C). If using a store-bought crust, prepare it according to package directions, typically by placing it in a 9-inch (23 cm) pie dish.
Scatter the crumbled blue cheese evenly over the bottom of the pie crust.
Sprinkle the chopped walnuts over the blue cheese.
In a medium bowl, whisk together the eggs, heavy cream, whole milk, black pepper, and nutmeg (if using) until well combined.
Carefully pour the egg mixture over the cheese and walnuts in the pie crust.
Bake for 35-40 minutes, or until the tart is golden brown and the center is set (a knife inserted near the center should come out clean).
Remove the tart from the oven and let it cool on a wire rack for at least 10-15 minutes before slicing and serving. It can be served warm or at room temperature.
tips: For an extra layer of flavor, lightly toast the walnuts in a dry pan for a few minutes before adding them to the tart.
This tart pairs wonderfully with a crisp green salad dressed with a simple vinaigrette, or alongside a hearty bowl of Wassail.
Leftovers can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 3 days and are delicious served cold or gently reheated.

apple-cakes.title: Traditional Wassail Apple Cakes
apple-cakes.intro: Old Twelfth Night Wassail is a traditional English custom, celebrated on January 17th, where communities gather in apple orchards to sing to the trees and scare away evil spirits, ensuring a bountiful harvest. These rustic Apple Cakes, infused with warming spices and chunks of apple, are a perfect treat to share during the festivities, offering comfort and a taste of the orchard's future bounty amidst the winter chill.
ingredients: 1/2 cup (113 g) unsalted butter, cold and cubed
1 large apple (about 1 cup / 150 g), peeled, cored, and finely diced (e.g., Granny Smith)
Optional: 1/4 cup (40 g) raisins or currants
